# What is the price?

*You'll need the order book, the touch, the mid and the walls (chapter 2), and the market maker and the backtest as
chapter 1 introduced them.*

## The story

In a backtest of Prosperity 4's round 1, our template traded Osmium in one market with three other teams' published
bots, all with resting orders. It lost 371 thousand credits. The cause, traced on one day against one of those bots,
was one number.

The template prices a product at its *wall mid*, the midpoint of the largest order on each side of the book. At tick
2,400 of day 0 the real wall on the bid side was 23 lots at 9,991. But a rival bot had a 40-lot bid resting at 9,906,
far below the touch, and 40 is more than 23. So the template took the rival's order for the wall, put its fair value
at 9,957 against the recorded wall mid of 10,001.5, 44.5 below it, and spent the session selling into bids that were
worth more than it thought. Its fair was 5 or more off on 36% of ticks
[(`IDEAS.md`, "The template against the teams' P4 traders in one market")]{.src}.

The fix was a different definition of "the wall": the first level from the top with at least 15 lots, which a large
order far from the touch can't capture. With it, the same market made +34 thousand credits instead of −371 thousand, and
on the products tested without rivals (Starfruit, Kelp, Osmium and Pepper Root) it stayed within 2.3% of the old rule [(`IDEAS.md`, "Wall-mid definitions")]{.src}.

## The idea

A market maker quotes around a *fair value*, its estimate of what the product is worth right now. Everything it earns
is measured from that number, so the first question on any market is how to estimate it from the book.

### The mid is noisy

The mid, halfway between the best bid and the best ask, is the obvious estimate, and on many books it is a poor one.
The touch is often made of small orders that come and go: a 2-lot bid appears one tick above the rest, and the mid
jumps half a tick without anything having changed. @fig-mid shows 300 ticks of Prosperity's Kelp.

![The mid and the wall mid over 300 ticks of Prosperity 3's Kelp. Data: `data/mid_and_wall.csv`, from the engine's
loader.](../figures/f04_mid_and_wall.png){#fig-mid
fig-alt="Two step lines over 300 ticks: the mid flickers by half a tick constantly; the wall mid moves in fewer, larger steps."}

### The walls know more

On Prosperity, Frankfurt Hedgehogs found that each product's large orders, the walls, came from market-making bots
that "appeared to know the true price and simply quoted rounded versions of it" (*their claim*, inferred from the
website's PnL) [(`references/prosperity3-frankfurt-hedgehogs/README.md:882-883`)]{.src}. Small orders from other bots
sit inside them. So the midpoint of the walls tracks the
value far better than the mid does:

::: {.eq speak="the wall mid is the midpoint of the largest order on each side of the book"}
$$\text{wall mid} = \frac{\text{bid wall} + \text{ask wall}}{2}$$
:::

That is a fact about Prosperity's generator, not a law of markets. On ABIDES, an independent simulator whose traders
have private views of a hidden value, every estimate we tried, mid, wall mid and the rest, was about 35 ticks from the
value on average, and smoothing them made it worse [(`IDEAS.md`, "An independent generator: ABIDES's RMSC04")]{.src}.
Which estimate works is something you measure on the day's data, not something you assume.

### Robust beats clever

The story's lesson is about robustness. "The largest level" is an argmax, and one outlier captures it: anyone who can
place a large order far from the touch moves your fair value. "The first level from the top with at least 15 lots",
the template's `sized_mid`, ignores anything behind the real wall. It cost at most 2.3% when the book was clean, and
saved everything when it wasn't. When other teams' bots share the book, or anyone has a reason to mislead you, prefer the
estimate a single order can't move.

### A fair value has a timescale

The other choice is how much history the estimate uses. A fair made from this tick's book alone follows every move; a
smoothed one averages over many ticks and ignores short ones. Neither is right in general. The right timescale is the
one over which deviations from the fair *come back*.

@fig-window shows how much that matters. On Prosperity 2's coconut coupon, an option (a contract whose value follows
another product, here coconuts), the template valued the coupon at a model price plus the coupon's gap from that
model, averaged with more weight on recent ticks (an exponential average over about `smile_window` ticks), and
traded what was left of the gap. With a 20-tick window that fast part
didn't come back: it drifted (its correlation from one tick to the next was 0.89), so fading it lost 267 thousand
credits. With a 5,000-tick window the same strategy made 442 thousand credits, its worst day +114 thousand
[(`IDEAS.md`, "Prosperity 2 round 4's coconut coupons with the template's options modes")]{.src}.

![One parameter, the fair's timescale, on Prosperity 2's coconut coupon (take_edge 0.5). Data: `data/smile_window.csv`,
from the IDEAS row's `arena.grid` command.](../figures/f08_smile_window.png){#fig-window
fig-alt="Line chart: profit in credits against the smile window on a log scale: minus 267 thousand at 20 ticks, plus 100 thousand at 200, 306 thousand at 1,000, 442 thousand at 5,000 and 418 thousand at 20,000."}

The check is cheap: before trading against a deviation, see whether it reverts at the horizon you trade it: its autocorrelation, or simply
whether fading it made money on each day separately.

::: {.callout-note title="If you know ML"}
A fair value is an estimator of a latent variable from noisy observations, and the usual lessons hold: prefer a
robust statistic when outliers can appear (a trimmed rule over an argmax), and choose the smoothing window to match the
signal's timescale, as you would a filter's bandwidth. Where it breaks: the outliers here can be adversarial, placed by
someone who profits from your error, and the latent "true value" may not exist at all on a market where informed
traders, not a generator, set the price.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="In the repo"}
- `fair_value` in `python/bots/template.py`, chosen per product by `PARAMS[...]["fair"]` (`mid`, `wall_mid`,
  `outer_mid`, `sized_mid`, `weighted_mid`, `hysteresis_mid`, `fixed`), with `wall_size` and `smoothing`.
- `arena.diagnose` says which estimate is least noisy on the day's data, and suggests a PARAMS entry with `--suggest`.
- The rows: "Wall-mid definitions", "The template against the teams' P4 traders in one market".
:::

`RUNBOOK.md`, "Each round", T+0:30: new products go into PARAMS by `references/wiki/concepts/reading-the-data-on-day-one.md`,
which maps each `diagnose` note to a choice of fair value and timescale.
:::
